extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, mathematics, and philosophy (advanced undergraduates / graduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the logical principles underlying number, arithmetic reasoning, inequalities, numerically definite syllogisms, and combinations/permutations, aimed at explaining when mathematical inference is valid. The text develops rules for treating units, substitution of equals, translation of logical conditions into numerical equations, and counting combinations under constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical agreement of quantities must remain unaltered
rubrics_metrics.description: In every arithmetical calculation the logical nature of the things numbered must remain unaltered; the specified logical agreement of the things must not be affected by the unspecified numerical differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is absurd for a calculation starting with length to give a result in hours; similarly, one should not deduce areas from lengths, masses from combination of volume and density, or momenta from mass and velocity unless logical units/interpretation justify it. Example: multiplying two linear feet does not arithmetically yield 'superficial feet' without changing the unit meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat in each calculation only objects of one nature (unit homogeneity)
rubrics_metrics.description: We treat in each calculation only objects of one nature; we cannot properly add heterogeneous units unless they are reducible to some common denominator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot add yards of cloth and pounds of sugar, nor conceive adding area to velocity. Different kinds must be kept distinct and treated numerically only in conjunction with their own kind. Chemists use separate equations per atom-kind; mathematicians treat compound symbols as representing separate simultaneous equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different units must never be substituted for one another
rubrics_metrics.description: Different units, insofar as their logical differences are specified, must never be substituted one for the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep distinct units separate in formal manipulations; apparent shorthand combining heterogeneous units actually represents multiple independent equations (e.g., equations mixing atom types or quaternions equate to several ordinary equations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical symbols obey laws of logic (commutativeness etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: If number arises out of logical conditions, number ought to obey the laws of logic; mathematical symbols do obey fundamental logical laws like commutativeness and analogous relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: AB = BA in logic corresponds to 2×3 = 3×2 in arithmetic; A + B = B + A corresponds to x + y = y + x. The properties of space are as indifferent in multiplication as in pure logical thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Simplicity and Unity (with presuppositions about units)
rubrics_metrics.description: The logical laws expressed as AA = A (Simplicity) and A ∥ A = A (Unity) hold with the understood presuppositions about distinct units; apparent exceptions arise from differing unit-discriminations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent failures (e.g., 2×2 ≠ 2 under naive analogy) are resolved by recognizing that the repeated units are discriminated (distinct instances). If the repeated instances were identical in meaning, the law of Unity would apply. Examples show how discrimination of units produces four distinct kinds when combining two binary classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of substitution / treating equals equally
rubrics_metrics.description: The universal principle of all reasoning in mathematics is that which allows substitution of like for like: in whatever relation one quantity stands to another, it stands in the same relation to the equal of that other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle underlies Euclid's axiom 'things equal to the same thing are equal to each other' and algebraic axioms (if equal quantities are added/multiplied by equal quantities, results are equal). Substitution is the active power enabling inferences across equalities and algebraic manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality is the condition of inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is equality there may be inference, but where there is not equality there cannot be inference; inference depends upon identities/equalities rather than mere differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three axioms (equal to same -> equal; equal+unequal -> unequal; things unequal to same thing may or may not be equal) summarized by 'whatever relation one quantity stands to another, it stands in the same relation to the equal of that other.' Examples: equalities enable inferences about lines, areas, forces, brightness; inequalities alone give no ground of inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoning by inequalities depends on underlying equalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments by inequalities can be represented in the form of equalities by introducing positive difference quantities; thus the force of inequality reasoning ultimately relies on equality expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express a > b as a = b + p where p is positive; chaining inequalities becomes substitution of such equalities (a = c + q + p). However, the converse fails: inequalities alone cannot prove equality between two quantities that are both > or < a third. Hence inequalities are imperfectly expressed equalities for rigorous inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetical reasoning relies on identities arising from numerical abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Although number arises from discrimination/difference, arithmetical reasoning is grounded on the unlimited series of identities produced by numerical abstraction; these identities enable inference despite differences in object qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: six people on six chairs—if only numerical discriminations are considered (marks to differentiate each chair and person), a resemblance in number allows inferences about occupancy. Definitions of numbers (e.g., 5 as 1+1+1+1+1) yield many non-arbitrary relations that become necessary inferences once a definition is fixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerically definite reasoning / numerically definite syllogism
rubrics_metrics.description: Some valid arguments combine logical and numerical reasoning (numerically definite syllogisms); given logical conditions and counts of objects in classes, arithmetic can determine counts in other classes or what additional data are needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References to De Morgan and Boole; demonstrations include representing class counts via bracketed symbols (e.g., (ABc) etc.) and solving problems such as 'for every man in the house there is a person who is aged; some men are not aged; it follows some persons in the house are not men' by algebraic manipulation of class counts with unknown positive quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical meaning of logical conditions: sameness of qualities -> sameness of numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Every logical proposition gives rise to a corresponding numerical equation: if A = B (identity of qualities) then (A) = (B) (numbers of A and B are equal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an equation of qualities can be drawn, a similar equation of numbers follows. However, this correspondence does not apply straightforwardly to negative propositions or inequalities (classes differing in qualities may yet agree in number).

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical Alphabet enables complete symbolic analysis of numerical problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The Logical Alphabet provides a system for decomposing and symbolically solving numerical-logical problems, representing the course the mind must follow in solving such questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though symbolical statements may be prolix, they track the necessary mental steps; examples include analytic solutions for voters objected to by two sides and for intersections of three classes via expansion and cancellation of bracketed class-count terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorics principle: number of varieties from n qualities is 2^n
rubrics_metrics.description: If n is the number of qualities, 2^n is the number of varieties of things which may be formed from them (assuming only logical conditions). Each new quality doubles the number of combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 4 qualities -> 16 combinations, 5 -> 32, 6 -> 64. Real-world restrictions (e.g., euphony rules in English) drastically reduce admissible combinations; counting admissible permutations under constraints can be difficult and is essential for inductive reasoning and probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of combinations is foundational for inductive science and parts of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of combinations applies numerical calculation to determine numbers of combinations under various conditions and underlies other sciences and branches of mathematics (algebraic form, probability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical notes: Pascal, Leibnitz, Bernoulli, Hindenburg worked on combinations; practical problems like counting allowable transpositions of protean verses demonstrate need for careful combinatorial analysis when constraints preserve sense and metre.
